implementation_notes: Swift concurrency supplies the shareable handle: Task is reference-shared, can be awaited from many callers and carries its own cancellation state; an actor isolates the registry, so the coalescing idiom is an actor holding a dictionary of in-flight Tasks keyed by the coalescing key. The ordering rule that makes it correct is an actor-reentrancy rule: the Task must be stored in the dictionary before the actor's first await, otherwise a second caller can enter the actor at that suspension point, miss the entry and start a duplicate. Await the stored Task outside the mutation, and remove the entry when the flight finishes - by identity, so a late cleanup cannot delete a newer flight.
pitfalls: Actor reentrancy: an actor suspends at await, so a second caller can enter before the first has stored its Task; insert the Task before any await or duplicates still happen.
Task cancellation is per-task: cancelling a caller's own task does not cancel the shared Task, but cancelling the shared Task fails every waiter - never hand it to a caller that might cancel it.
Remove the entry by identity (a reference-typed entry, as above), not by key alone: a later call may have installed a new flight by the time an earlier waiter cleans up.
A stored Task retains its closure and captured values until it completes; unbounded key cardinality keeps completed flights alive unless every path removes the entry.
A waiter cancelled while awaiting surfaces CancellationError locally while the flight keeps running: distinguish 'I stopped waiting' from 'the flight failed'.
